unit.name: Engineering Materials & Their Properties
unit.subtitle: The six material families on the spec, the physical properties that define them, and how destructive and non-destructive testing prove a material is fit for purpose.

lessons.title: Ferrous & Non-Ferrous Metals
lessons.description: Mild steel, stainless steel, tool steel, brass, copper and aluminium — properties and engineering applications.
lessons.content_html:
The Two Metal Families

All metals used in engineering can be placed into one of two families. The classification rule is simple: does the metal contain iron? Ferrous metals contain iron. Non-ferrous metals do not. This matters in engineering for three reasons: ferrous metals are generally magnetic (useful for sorting in recycling and for electromagnetic applications); ferrous metals corrode through rusting when exposed to oxygen and moisture; and the two families have quite different density and conductivity profiles, which drives material selection for specific products.

Key Fact

The rule: ferrous metals contain iron; non-ferrous metals do not. Ferrous metals are magnetic and can rust. Non-ferrous metals do not contain iron, are not magnetic, and generally do not rust in the same way. A simple magnetism test can separate the two families.

Ferrous Metals

Mild Steel

Mild steel is iron with a low carbon content (typically below 0.3% by weight). It is the most widely used engineering metal. Its combination of good tensile strength, toughness and weldability makes it suitable for a very wide range of products. It can be pressed, rolled, bent and welded without cracking under normal workshop conditions. However, mild steel rusts readily when exposed to moisture and must be protected by painting, galvanising (coating with zinc) or another surface treatment. Common uses include car body panels, structural beams, pipes, sheet metal enclosures and bicycle frames.

Stainless Steel

Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with chromium (and typically nickel) added. The chromium content makes the surface corrosion-resistant — it forms a thin oxide layer that prevents the iron beneath from rusting. Stainless steel does not need painting to survive in moist environments. It is harder and more expensive to machine than mild steel. Common uses include kitchen sinks, cutlery, surgical instruments, food-processing equipment and the exterior cladding of some buildings.

Tool Steel

Tool steel has a higher carbon content than mild steel and can be hardened through heat treatment processes such as quenching (rapid cooling). The result is a very hard material that holds a sharp cutting edge. This makes it suitable for cutting tools, drills, punches, dies and blades. The trade-off is that tool steel is more brittle than mild steel — it can fracture under impact loading rather than deforming. It is generally not welded in service because welding disrupts the heat-treated microstructure.

Rusting is an electrochemical process in which iron reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide (rust). Unlike the oxide layer on aluminium or the patina on copper, rust does not form a protective barrier — it is porous and continues to allow oxygen and water through to attack the metal beneath. Left untreated, rust will eventually weaken a mild steel component significantly. Engineers prevent rusting by painting (blocking contact with air and moisture), galvanising (zinc coating — zinc corrodes preferentially, protecting the steel beneath), applying plastic coatings, or choosing a different material such as stainless steel or aluminium for applications where rusting would be a serious problem.

Non-Ferrous Metals

Brass

Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. The proportions vary by grade, but typical brass is roughly 70% copper and 30% zinc by weight. Brass machines easily, resists corrosion well and has an attractive gold-like appearance. It is used for plumbing fittings (taps, valves, pipe connectors), musical instrument components, electrical connectors and decorative hardware such as door handles. Brass is not as strong as steel for structural applications but is chosen where its corrosion resistance and machinability are more valuable than raw strength.

Copper

Copper is notable in engineering for its outstanding electrical conductivity — it is the standard material for electrical wiring in buildings, appliances and vehicles precisely because it allows current to flow with very low resistance. Copper also has excellent thermal conductivity, making it useful for heat exchangers and water pipes. It is relatively soft and ductile (can be drawn into fine wire or bent into pipe without cracking). Copper corrodes slowly in air, forming a green patina (copper carbonate) that protects the surface beneath. Common uses include electrical cables, water distribution pipes, the coils of electric motors, and printed circuit board tracks.

Key Fact

Copper is the standard material for electrical wiring because it has outstanding electrical conductivity — current flows through it with minimal resistance. It is also ductile enough to be drawn into fine wire and shaped without breaking.

Aluminium

Aluminium is the most widely used non-ferrous engineering metal. Its key advantages are low density (making it much lighter than steel for the same volume), good corrosion resistance (it forms a thin protective oxide layer naturally) and adequate strength for many applications, especially when alloyed with elements such as silicon, magnesium or copper. It conducts electricity and heat well (though not as well as copper). Aluminium does not rust — it oxidises, but the oxide layer is stable and adherent. Common uses include aircraft structures, vehicle body panels and engine components, food and drink cans, window frames, bicycle frames and smartphone casings.

Material selection requires matching the material’s properties to the engineering requirements of the product. A bicycle frame needs high tensile strength (to resist being pulled apart under load) and low density (to reduce weight) — aluminium alloy meets both. A kitchen sink needs corrosion resistance and ease of cleaning — stainless steel is the standard answer. Electrical wiring needs high conductivity and ductility — copper. Cutting tools need hardness and edge retention — tool steel. Decorative plumbing fittings need corrosion resistance and machinability — brass. Exam questions often present a product and ask you to justify a specific material choice by linking properties to requirements. Use the pattern: state the property, link it to the product requirement, name the material that provides it.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Material selection questions nearly always ask you to ‘justify’ or ‘explain’ your choice. Naming the metal alone earns very few marks. You must connect a property to the engineering requirement: ‘Stainless steel is chosen for the kitchen sink because its chromium content makes it corrosion-resistant, meaning it will not rust in the wet environment of a kitchen.’ For the ferrous/non-ferrous distinction, a common exam trap is to describe aluminium as ‘like steel’ because it is silver-coloured — always state the iron-content rule to distinguish them clearly. Remember: mild steel, stainless steel and tool steel are ferrous; brass, copper and aluminium are non-ferrous.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ferrous metals contain iron and are typically magnetic; non-ferrous metals do not contain iron and are not magnetic. Ferrous metals rust; non-ferrous metals generally do not.
  • Ferrous metals on the spec: mild steel (structural, weldable), stainless steel (corrosion-resistant, cutlery/sinks), tool steel (hardenable, cutting tools). Non-ferrous: brass (corrosion-resistant, plumbing), copper (high conductivity, wiring), aluminium (lightweight, aircraft/vehicle panels).
  • Material selection links a property to a product requirement. State the material, name the relevant property, and explain why that property makes it suitable for the specific application.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is choosing a material for a bicycle frame. Explain why aluminium alloy is often preferred over mild steel for this application.

practice_questions.text: A teacher is equipping a school engineering workshop with tools and equipment. Explain why tool steel is used for drill bits and cutting tools rather than mild steel. In your answer, refer to the relevant material properties.

Mastering: Two or more well-developed points covering hardness (tool steel can be hardened by heat treatment to hold a cutting edge that mild steel cannot maintain), edge retention under repeated use, and the trade-off (tool steel is more brittle so a drill bit that is incorrectly used can snap — mild steel would deform rather than fracture, but would blunt too quickly to be useful as a cutting tool).
Secure: Two engineering points with clear explanation of properties and their relevance to cutting tool performance.
Developing: One developed point or two superficial points without full engineering reasoning.
Emerging: General statements about tool steel being harder without explaining the mechanism or trade-off.

lessons.title: Plastics, Smart Materials & Composites
lessons.description: Thermoplastics, thermosetting plastics, smart materials and composites — properties and engineering uses.
lessons.content_html:
Three More Material Families

After ferrous and non-ferrous metals, the specification introduces three further material families: plastics (divided into two distinct types), smart materials, and composites. Each has a different internal structure that determines how it behaves and what it can be used for. Getting the families right matters in the exam — a common mistake is to label any modern or technical-sounding material as ‘smart’. The definition of a smart material is precise, and you need to apply it correctly.

Key Fact

A smart material is a material whose property changes reversibly in response to an external stimulus. The stimulus triggers the change; remove the stimulus and the material returns to its original state. This reversibility is the key discriminator. Examples: thermochromic pigments (change colour with temperature) and shape-memory alloys such as Nitinol (return to a remembered shape when heated).

Thermoplastics

Thermoplastics are polymers made of long molecular chains. The chains are held together by relatively weak forces rather than permanent chemical bonds between them. When a thermoplastic is heated, the chains become mobile and the material softens. When it cools, the chains lock together again and the material hardens. This heating-softening-cooling-hardening cycle can be repeated many times without permanently degrading the material, which is why thermoplastics can be recycled.

The three thermoplastics on the specification are acrylic (commonly known by trade names but properly called poly(methyl methacrylate)), nylon (a polyamide, tough and low-friction) and high-impact polystyrene (HIPS, impact-resistant and easy to vacuum-form). Acrylic is used for display cases, light diffusers and the rear lights of vehicles; its transparency and optical clarity make it a glass substitute in many applications. Nylon is used for gears, bearings and textile fibres because of its toughness and low coefficient of friction. HIPS is used in packaging, school engineering projects and domestic appliance linings because it is easy to vacuum-form into complex shapes at relatively low cost.

Thermosetting plastics undergo a different process. During manufacture, the liquid polymer is poured into a mould and heat or a chemical catalyst causes the chains to form permanent cross-links to each other. This produces a rigid, three-dimensional network structure. Because the cross-links are permanent chemical bonds, the material cannot be re-softened by heating — applying heat will cause it to char or decompose rather than melt. This is why thermosetting plastics cannot be recycled in the same way as thermoplastics.

The two thermosetting plastics on the specification are urea formaldehyde and silicone (also written ‘silicon’ in some engineering contexts, though strictly the material is silicone — a polymer). Urea formaldehyde is a hard, brittle material used for electrical fittings (plug casings, switch housings) and kitchen worktop laminates. It is chosen because it does not soften or distort at the temperatures these applications encounter. Silicone has very different properties: it remains flexible across a wide temperature range and is chemically resistant. It is used for baking moulds, sealants, medical-grade implants and gaskets. Both are permanently set and cannot be re-moulded.

Smart Materials

Smart materials are defined by their response to a stimulus. Two types are on the specification. The first is thermochromic pigments and inks. These contain molecules whose structure rearranges at a critical temperature, causing them to absorb different wavelengths of light and therefore appear a different colour. Below the critical temperature the pigment appears one colour; above it, another. Remove the heat source and the pigment returns to its original colour. Applications include novelty mugs that reveal an image when hot liquid is poured in, baby bath thermometers that change colour to indicate safe water temperature, and packaging that indicates whether a frozen product has been thawed and refrozen (a food safety application).

The second smart material on the specification is Nitinol (also written as nitinol wire), a shape-memory alloy made from nickel and titanium. It can be deformed at low temperature and will hold the deformed shape. Heat it above its transformation temperature and it returns to the shape it was set to during manufacture. This shape-memory effect is reversible and reliable over many cycles. Engineering applications include stents (medical devices inserted into arteries — the stent is compressed for insertion, then expands to its set shape at body temperature), eyeglass frames that spring back after bending, and actuators in control systems where a linear movement is needed in response to a temperature change.

Key Fact

Nitinol is a smart material because its shape-change behaviour is triggered by a stimulus (heat) and is reversible (it returns to its set shape every time the temperature rises above the transformation point). Carbon fibre is not a smart material — it is a composite. Smart materials change a property in response to a stimulus; composites combine two materials to create a new set of properties.

A composite material combines a reinforcement and a matrix. The reinforcement provides strength or stiffness; the matrix holds the reinforcement in place and transfers loads to it. The resulting material has properties that neither constituent has alone — this is the engineering rationale for using a composite rather than a single material.

Carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) consists of woven or laid carbon fibre strands embedded in a polymer resin matrix (typically epoxy resin). Carbon fibres are stiff and strong in tension; the resin matrix holds them in position and protects them from damage. The resulting composite has an exceptionally high strength-to-weight ratio — significantly stronger than steel for the same mass. It is used in aircraft structures (reducing weight and fuel consumption), Formula One car bodies, high-performance bicycle frames and sports equipment such as tennis rackets and rowing oars. It is expensive and difficult to repair compared with metals, but where weight saving is critical, the cost is justified.

Kevlar (an aramid fibre composite) has a different property profile. Kevlar fibres are extremely strong in tension and highly resistant to impact. A woven Kevlar fabric does not stretch easily under sudden impact loads — energy is absorbed and distributed across the fibres rather than being concentrated at a point. This makes Kevlar the standard material for ballistic protection vests, helmets, cut-resistant gloves and the reinforcement layer in vehicle tyres. Like CFRP, Kevlar cannot be melted and reshaped — its composite structure is permanent.

Selecting the Right Polymer or Composite

Material selection for plastics and composites follows the same logic as for metals: match the material’s properties to the engineering requirements. An electrical fitting needs a material that does not soften at operating temperatures and does not conduct electricity — urea formaldehyde (thermosetting, electrically insulating, heat-stable) is correct. A product that must be recycled at end of life should use a thermoplastic rather than a thermosetting plastic. A product requiring very low weight and high strength — an aircraft panel, a racing car component — may justify the high cost of carbon fibre reinforced polymer. A product requiring impact and cut resistance for personal protection — a ballistic vest — uses Kevlar.

For smart material applications, the trigger must match the intended use. Thermochromic pigments are appropriate where temperature indication is needed at the point of use. Nitinol is appropriate where a reliable, reversible mechanical movement is needed in response to a specific temperature change. Neither thermochromic pigments nor Nitinol are structural materials — they are functional materials responding to stimuli, not load-bearing elements of a structure.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error on materials questions is calling carbon fibre a smart material. Always define smart materials first: ‘A smart material changes a property reversibly in response to a stimulus.’ Carbon fibre does not change its properties in response to a stimulus — it is a composite of carbon fibres in a resin matrix. For thermoplastic vs thermosetting questions, the discriminator is always the cross-linked structure: ‘Thermosetting plastics cannot be recycled because heating does not re-soften them — their cross-linked bonds are permanent.’ For 4-mark and 6-mark questions on material choice, always give the material name, the relevant property, and the product requirement it meets.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Thermoplastics (acrylic, nylon, HIPS) can be recycled — polymer chains re-soften on heating. Thermosetting plastics (urea formaldehyde, silicone) cannot — cross-linked structure is permanent.
  • Smart materials change a property reversibly in response to a stimulus: thermochromic pigments change colour with temperature; Nitinol (shape-memory alloy) returns to a set shape when heated. Carbon fibre is a composite, not a smart material.
  • Composites combine reinforcement and matrix to create properties neither constituent has alone. Carbon fibre reinforced polymer offers a high strength-to-weight ratio; Kevlar offers outstanding impact and cut resistance.

lessons.title: Physical Properties & Selecting Materials for Engineered Products
lessons.description: Ten physical properties explained and applied to mobile phones, alarms, bicycles and play areas.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Physical Properties?

Every material has a set of physical properties — measurable characteristics that describe how it behaves under real-world conditions. When an engineer selects a material for a product, they match the properties of available materials to the demands the product will face. Get the match wrong and the product fails; get it right and the product works reliably throughout its designed lifetime.

The specification lists ten physical properties you must be able to describe, distinguish and apply. This lesson covers all ten, then shows how they combine when selecting materials for four specific products: mobile phones, home security alarms, bicycles and children’s play area equipment.

Key Fact

The ten physical properties are: tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, toughness, malleability, ductility, electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, corrosion resistance and elasticity. Examiners expect you to describe each one precisely — they are not synonyms.

Strength: Tensile and Compressive

Tensile strength is a material’s ability to resist a pulling (tensile) force without breaking. A steel cable supporting a suspension bridge must have high tensile strength — the force in the cable is always a pull. Steel and most metals have high tensile strength; ceramics and cast iron have relatively low tensile strength because they are brittle.

Compressive strength is a material’s ability to resist a squeezing (compressive) force without deforming or cracking. Concrete has high compressive strength, which is why it is used for columns and foundations. In contrast, concrete has low tensile strength — steel reinforcing bars are embedded to compensate for this weakness.

Hardness is a material’s resistance to surface indentation or scratching. A hard material like tool steel resists the cutting forces of a drill bit; a glass screen is hard enough to resist scratching by keys. However, hardness and toughness are different properties — a hard material is not necessarily tough.

Toughness is a material’s ability to absorb energy and resist fracture under impact. Glass is hard but not tough — it resists scratching but shatters under impact. Mild steel is both hard enough and tough: it can absorb an impact without cracking. A bicycle frame material must be tough so that a sudden bump or collision does not cause the frame to fracture suddenly.

Exam tip on this distinction: if a question asks why a product needs toughness rather than just hardness, your answer must mention impact energy absorption and resistance to fracture — not just resistance to scratching.

Malleability and Ductility

Malleability is the ability of a material to be shaped by compressive forces — rolled into sheets, hammered into shapes, or pressed into moulds — without cracking. Copper and aluminium are both malleable, making them suitable for pressing into complex shapes such as car body panels or electrical connectors.

Ductility is the ability of a material to be stretched into a wire or rod without breaking. Copper is highly ductile: it can be drawn into the thin wires used inside electrical cables. A material can be malleable without being ductile, and vice versa, so the exam expects you to use the correct term for the correct process.

Conductivity: Electrical and Thermal

Electrical conductivity is the ease with which a material allows an electric current to flow through it. Copper is an excellent electrical conductor — it is the most widely used material for wiring. Plastics are electrical insulators: they have very low conductivity and are used to coat cables and encase electrical components to prevent electric shock.

Thermal conductivity is the ease with which a material allows heat to flow through it. Metals generally conduct heat well; plastics and ceramics are poor thermal conductors. These two conductivities often move in the same direction (metals conduct both electricity and heat), but this is not always the case, so treat them as separate properties.

Key Fact

Copper is used for electrical wiring because it has very high electrical conductivity — it allows current to flow with very low resistance. Its ductility means it can be drawn into thin wire. Both properties must be stated when justifying copper as a wiring material.

Corrosion Resistance and Environmental Degradation

Corrosion resistance is a material’s ability to resist chemical attack by substances in its environment, most commonly water, oxygen, acids or salts. Stainless steel is chosen for outdoor structures partly because its chromium content creates a protective oxide layer that resists corrosion. Mild steel, by contrast, corrodes readily in damp air unless it is painted, plated or coated.

Environmental degradation is the broader process by which materials deteriorate due to environmental exposure over time. UV light breaks down many plastics, causing them to become brittle and discolour. Temperature cycling can fatigue metals. Engineers working on outdoor products — such as play area equipment — must account for all the environmental factors the product will face over its working life.

Elasticity

Elasticity is the ability of a material to return to its original shape after a deforming force is removed. A spring steel returns to its shape after being compressed or stretched. Rubber is also highly elastic. When a material is stretched beyond its elastic limit, it deforms permanently — this is called plastic deformation. Engineers must ensure that materials in springs and flexible components operate within their elastic limit in normal service.

Mobile phone casing and screen: The casing must be hard (to resist scratches from keys and coins), tough (to survive drops), and have low electrical conductivity (to be safe to handle). The screen must also be hard and have good optical clarity; some glass formulations are engineered to be tougher than standard glass.

Home security alarm housing and sensor: The outer casing must have good corrosion resistance and resist environmental degradation (UV, damp) because it may be mounted outside. Electrical components inside require materials with high electrical conductivity for wiring and low electrical conductivity for the casing — to prevent short circuits. The casing must be tough enough to resist deliberate tampering.

Bicycle frame: The frame must have high tensile strength (pedalling and rider weight create pulling forces in the frame tubes), good toughness (to survive kerb drops and collisions without fracturing), and low density so that the bike remains light. Aluminium alloy frames balance these requirements: aluminium is not as strong as steel, but it is much lighter, so larger-diameter tubes are used to compensate. Good corrosion resistance is also important for a product used outdoors in wet conditions.

Children’s play area equipment: Safety is the primary concern. Materials must have high toughness (impact from children climbing and falling), good corrosion resistance (outdoor environment, rain), resistance to environmental degradation (UV light degrades plastics over time), and smooth surfaces to prevent injuries. Rubber impact surfaces beneath equipment also rely on high elasticity to absorb landing impacts safely.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘explain’ why a material is chosen, you must link the property to the product’s function — not just name the property. For example: “Aluminium is chosen for the bicycle frame because its low density reduces the overall weight of the bike, making it easier for the rider to accelerate and climb hills.” A ‘describe’ question only needs the property stated; an ‘explain’ question needs the reasoning. Watch for the command word.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The ten physical properties — tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, toughness, malleability, ductility, electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, corrosion resistance and elasticity — are distinct. Never use them as synonyms.
  • Material selection matches properties to product demands: a bicycle frame needs tensile strength and toughness; a phone casing needs hardness and electrical insulation; play area equipment needs toughness and corrosion resistance.
  • Top-band answers link the chosen property to the specific function of the product part — stating the property alone is not enough for an ‘explain’ question.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'toughness'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: ability to absorb energy and resist fracture/cracking under impact. Accept equivalent wording focusing on impact resistance and not fracturing.

practice_questions.text: Give two physical properties that would be important when selecting a material for a bicycle frame. For each property, give one reason why it is needed.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per property + reason pair (max 2 marks). Accept any two from: tensile strength (resists pulling forces from pedalling / rider weight); toughness (absorbs impact without fracturing); corrosion resistance (used outdoors in wet conditions); low density (not a physical property in the same list — do not award for density alone, but award if framed as 'light material needed for easy acceleration'). Two clear property + reason pairs required.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between malleability and ductility.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clearly distinguishes both terms with accurate definitions and links each to a manufacturing process (e.g. malleability — shaped by compression/rolling/hammering; ductility — drawn into wire/rod). Secure: Defines both terms accurately but without naming a specific process. Developing: Defines one term correctly. Emerging: Attempts a description but conflates the two terms.

practice_questions.text: A home security alarm is fitted on the outside wall of a house. Explain why corrosion resistance and resistance to environmental degradation are both important properties for the alarm housing.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains both properties with clear cause-and-effect reasoning — e.g. corrosion resistance prevents chemical reaction with rain/moisture that would weaken or damage the housing; environmental degradation resistance (e.g. UV light from sunlight breaking down the plastic) prevents the housing becoming brittle or discoloured over time. Distinguishes between the two properties. Secure: Explains both properties but the distinction between chemical corrosion and broader environmental degradation is not fully drawn. Developing: Explains one property correctly with a reason. Emerging: Names properties without explanation.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is choosing between mild steel and aluminium alloy for a children's climbing frame. Explain which material would be more suitable, referring to at least two physical properties in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Compares both materials across at least two relevant properties (e.g. corrosion resistance — aluminium forms a protective oxide layer, mild steel corrodes without treatment; toughness — both can be tough but steel is generally tougher; weight/density — aluminium is lighter, which reduces foundation load and is safer in the event of tipping). Makes a justified choice of material with clear engineering reasoning. Secure: Discusses two properties and makes a choice, but the reasoning for one property is less developed. Developing: Mentions two properties but treats them as advantages without comparing materials. Emerging: Makes a choice without property-based justification.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the physical properties required for the screen material of a modern mobile phone. In your answer, consider both the properties needed and the limitations of any material chosen.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies multiple relevant properties (hardness to resist scratching; toughness to survive drops without shattering; optical transparency; electrical insulation for safe handling; low thermal conductivity to avoid heat discomfort). Discusses at least one limitation or trade-off (e.g. increasing hardness through tempering or special formulation can reduce toughness; thicker glass improves toughness but adds weight). Reaches a justified conclusion about how engineers balance competing demands. Secure: Identifies three or more properties with explanation, makes one trade-off point, reaches a conclusion. Developing: Identifies two properties with some explanation; no trade-off discussed. Emerging: Names one or two properties without developed explanation.

lessons.title: Testing Materials — Destructive & Non-Destructive
lessons.description: Destructive and non-destructive tests for tensile strength, hardness, toughness and conductivity.
lessons.content_html:
Why Test Materials?

Before an engineer specifies a material for a product, they need evidence that it will perform as required. Material testing provides that evidence. Some tests are carried out during the design phase, to check that a chosen material meets the specification. Others are used in production quality control, to check that every batch of material supplied to the factory has the properties expected. The type of test chosen depends on what property needs to be measured — and whether the sample being tested can be sacrificed.

Key Fact

Destructive testing (DT) damages or destroys the sample to obtain a measurement. It cannot be used on a finished product that is going into service. Non-destructive testing (NDT) measures properties without permanently harming the sample — the part can still be used after testing.

Destructive Testing: Tensile Test

A tensile test measures tensile strength. The sample is machined into a standardised ‘dog-bone’ shape so that the test section has a known cross-sectional area. It is gripped in a tensile testing machine and a gradually increasing pulling force is applied until the sample fractures. The maximum force sustained before fracture, divided by the original cross-sectional area, gives the tensile strength. The sample is destroyed in the process.

The tensile test also reveals ductility. As the force increases, the sample stretches. The engineer measures how much the sample elongates before it fractures: a ductile material will neck (form a visible waist) and stretch significantly; a brittle material will fracture suddenly with very little stretching. Plotting force against extension produces a stress–strain curve, which shows the elastic limit, yield point and ultimate tensile strength of the material.

Destructive Testing: Hardness Test

Hardness testing uses an indenter — a hard ball or diamond-tipped cone — pressed into the surface of the sample under a controlled force. The size of the indent left in the surface is measured. A smaller indent means a harder material. Common hardness scales include the Brinell test (steel ball) and the Vickers test (diamond pyramid). Although the indenter leaves a mark in the surface, the sample is generally not destroyed, so hardness testing is sometimes described as semi-destructive. For exam purposes, the specification lists it under destructive testing, so classify it accordingly.

Destructive Testing: Toughness Test

A Charpy impact test measures toughness. A notched sample is placed horizontally on two supports and struck by a heavy pendulum. (Note: in the related Izod test the specimen is clamped vertically at one end — this is the key difference between the two methods.) The height the pendulum swings to after impact tells the engineer how much energy the material absorbed — a tough material absorbs more energy and the pendulum does not swing as high on the follow-through. The sample is fractured in the test. This test is used to check that structural steels maintain their toughness at low temperatures, since some metals become brittle in cold conditions.

Malleability test: A sample is repeatedly hammered or rolled while being observed for cracking. A malleable material can be worked without cracking; a brittle material will crack early in the test. The test is destructive because the sample is deformed in the process.

Ductility test (cup and cone / wire draw): The tensile test already provides ductility data through percentage elongation measurements. A separate bend test — bending a sample through a set angle — also checks ductility: a ductile sample bends without cracking, a brittle one fractures.

Elasticity test: A spring or sample is loaded to a known force and the extension is measured. The load is then removed. If the sample returns to its original length, it behaved elastically within the test range. If the sample remains permanently deformed, it was loaded beyond its elastic limit. The test can be conducted without fracturing the sample if it is kept below the elastic limit.

Conductivity Testing

Electrical conductivity is tested by passing a known current through a sample of defined dimensions and measuring the voltage across it. Using Ohm’s law (V = IR), the resistance can be calculated, which is the inverse of conductivity. A multimeter is a common workshop tool used to measure resistance in materials and components. This test does not destroy the sample, so it is a non-destructive test.

Non-Destructive Testing: The Core Principle

NDT methods leave the test sample intact and usable. This matters enormously in engineering practice because many parts — the welds on a bridge, the fuselage skin of an aircraft, the gas pipe below a city street — cannot be sacrificed for a destructive test. NDT allows engineers to check for internal flaws, cracks or weaknesses without cutting the part open. The most important NDT methods at this level are visual inspection and ultrasonic testing.

Scenario: A manufacturer produces a batch of steel cable for a new suspension bridge. They want to verify that the cable meets its tensile strength specification before installation. After installation, the bridge maintenance team wants to check the cables annually for internal corrosion and micro-cracks.

Before installation — destructive tensile test: A sample of cable from the batch is pulled to fracture in a tensile testing machine. This confirms the tensile strength meets the specification. The tested sample is destroyed, but because it is taken from the production batch rather than from the actual bridge cable, this is acceptable. The tested sample cannot be used in the bridge.

After installation — non-destructive ultrasonic test: Sound waves are passed through the installed cable. Any crack or void inside the cable reflects the sound waves back differently from solid metal. The maintenance team can detect internal flaws without cutting the cable out of the bridge. The cable remains in service throughout the test.

Key principle: Use DT to characterise material properties before the product goes into service. Use NDT to inspect finished parts and products that must remain intact and in service.

Key Fact

The fundamental reason to choose NDT over DT is that the in-service part cannot be sacrificed. A weld in a live gas pipeline cannot be cut out for a destructive test; an ultrasonic scan checks for cracks non-destructively. Top-band exam answers connect the choice of test to whether the product can be sacrificed.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A common exam mistake is to say destructive testing ‘breaks the sample’ and leave it there. You must also say why this matters for the product — namely, that the tested sample cannot go into service. For ‘explain’ questions on NDT, state that the part remains intact and can continue to be used after testing.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Destructive testing (tensile test, impact test, hardness test) permanently damages or destroys the sample but gives precise measurements of properties such as tensile strength, toughness and hardness.
  • Non-destructive testing leaves the sample intact and is used on in-service parts that cannot be sacrificed — such as welds, pipelines and structural cables.
  • Choosing between DT and NDT depends on whether the part being tested can be sacrificed and whether the test is part of quality control on a new batch or inspection of an existing product.

practice_questions.text: Name one destructive test used to measure the tensile strength of a material.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: tensile test / tensile strength test. Accept equivalent naming.

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of non-destructive testing over destructive testing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each (max 2 marks) for any two from: the part/sample remains intact after testing; can be used on parts that are already in service / installed; allows 100% inspection of a production run without losing product; can test finished, assembled products. Do not accept vague answers like 'it is better'.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a Charpy impact test is carried out and what the result tells an engineer about the material.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes the notched sample being struck by a swinging pendulum; the height the pendulum reaches after impact is measured; a higher follow-through swing means less energy was absorbed, so the material is less tough. Secure: Describes the pendulum striking a sample and measuring energy absorbed; may not mention the notch or the follow-through height clearly. Developing: States that it tests toughness and involves striking with a pendulum, but lacks detail of the energy measurement. Emerging: Names the test without describing the method.

practice_questions.text: A quality control engineer receives a new batch of mild steel sheets from a supplier. Explain why a tensile test would be used rather than an ultrasonic inspection to check the material properties of the batch.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that tensile testing directly measures tensile strength (the mechanical property needed for quality control); the batch sample is sacrificed but this is acceptable as it is a small sample from the batch, not the product itself; ultrasonic inspection detects internal flaws/cracks in completed parts but does not measure tensile strength. Secure: Explains that tensile testing measures strength directly and gives quantified results; notes that a sample can be taken from the batch for destruction. Developing: States that tensile testing is appropriate for measuring strength but does not explain why NDT would be unsuitable or why the sample can be sacrificed. Emerging: Names tensile testing without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why non-destructive testing is essential for checking the welds on a suspension bridge cable after the bridge has been built and opened.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that the cable cannot be removed from the bridge or destroyed because it is a structural component carrying load; NDT (e.g. ultrasonic testing) can detect internal cracks or voids in the weld without cutting the cable or taking it out of service; the bridge remains safe and open during inspection. Secure: Explains that the cable must remain in place and NDT allows inspection without damage; may not explain the consequence of using DT. Developing: States that NDT does not damage the part but does not explain why damaging the cable would be unacceptable. Emerging: Names NDT without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and limitations of destructive testing when used to ensure the quality of engineering products leaving a factory. In your answer, refer to specific tests.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Discusses DT advantages (precise measurements of properties such as tensile strength via tensile test, toughness via impact test; gives quantified data for quality approval; methods are well-established). Discusses limitations (sample is destroyed so cannot go into service; cannot test every unit in a production run, only samples; cannot be used on in-service parts; selection of samples introduces statistical uncertainty). Refers to at least two specific tests by name. Reaches a conclusion on how DT and NDT are used together. Secure: Discusses advantages and one limitation with specific test named; conclusion present. Developing: Identifies advantages and one limitation; one specific test named. Emerging: Makes general points without referring to specific tests or drawing a reasoned conclusion.

glossary_terms.definition: Testing that permanently damages or destroys the sample in the process of measuring a material property.
Testing that measures material properties without permanently damaging the sample, so the part can still be used.
A destructive test in which a sample is pulled apart by an increasing tensile force until it fractures, measuring the material's tensile strength.
A test in which a hard indenter is pressed into a material surface under a known force, and the size of the indent is used to calculate hardness.
A destructive impact test in which a notched sample is struck by a swinging pendulum, and the energy absorbed is used to measure toughness.
The process of testing materials or products during production to ensure they meet the required specification before use.
